title: Apply Self Management through the Concepts of Positive Self-esteem and Resiliency

lessons.title: Understanding self-esteem
lessons.html:
How you see yourself shapes how you work

Self-esteem is the opinion you have of yourself: whether you believe you have value, can learn and can handle what life brings. It is not the same as being proud or loud. A person with healthy self-esteem respects themselves and others, accepts their strengths and weaknesses, and is willing to try new things.

Signs of healthy and low self-esteem

Healthy self-esteemLow self-esteem
Speaks up with ideas or concernsStays silent even when something is wrong
Accepts feedback and learns from mistakesTakes feedback as a personal attack, or blames others
Sets goals and works towards themBelieves nothing will ever change
Can say no politelyAgrees to everything to be liked
Respects othersPuts others down to feel better

Where self-esteem comes from

Our self-esteem is shaped by family, community, school, experiences at work, and the messages we hear about ourselves. A worker who was told for years that they are stupid may start to believe it. The good news is that self-esteem can be built at any age.

Self-talk

We all talk to ourselves in our minds. Negative self-talk sounds like I always mess up or I will never be a supervisor. Positive, realistic self-talk sounds like I made a mistake with the feed records, but I can learn the correct method. Notice your self-talk and replace unfair thoughts with fair, realistic ones.

Self-esteem at work

On a farm or in a poultry plant, people with healthy self-esteem report safety problems, ask questions when they do not understand, help new workers and take pride in quality work.

lessons.title: Building self-esteem and self-management
lessons.html:
Practical ways to grow

Know yourself

Write down your strengths: perhaps you are reliable, good with animals, careful with records or good at calming down a team. Write down areas you want to improve. Ask someone you trust for their view. Knowing yourself is the start of managing yourself.

Set goals

Goals give direction. Use SMART goals: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound. For example: By the end of March I will complete my forklift licence training, or I will save R200 every month for six months. Break big goals into small steps and celebrate when you reach each one.

Manage yourself

  • Time: arrive on time, plan your tasks, keep promises.
  • Emotions: when you feel angry, pause, breathe and think before you respond.
  • Money: make a budget, avoid unnecessary debt and loan sharks.
  • Health: sleep, eat well, avoid alcohol and drug abuse, exercise.
  • Learning: take opportunities for training and ask questions.

Assertive communication

Being assertive means stating your needs and views clearly and respectfully, without being passive (saying nothing) or aggressive (shouting, threatening). An assertive statement uses I: I feel worried when the guard is left off the machine. I would like us to put it back before we start.

Respecting others

Healthy self-esteem includes respecting others' dignity. Avoid gossip, insults and discrimination. Recognise good work by co-workers. A respectful team builds everyone's self-esteem.

Example

Sipho is asked to work a double shift again. Instead of agreeing and feeling resentful, or refusing angrily, he says: I worked late twice this week and I am very tired. I can do Saturday, but not tonight.

lessons.title: Resilience: bouncing back
lessons.html:
Coping with setbacks and stress

Resilience is the ability to recover from difficulties and keep going. Farm and processing work brings many setbacks: drought, a disease outbreak that closes a house, retrenchments, injury, family problems, or not getting a promotion. Resilient people still feel pain and disappointment, but they find ways to adapt.

Habits of resilient people

  • Accept what cannot be changed and focus energy on what can.
  • Keep perspective: one bad day or one mistake does not define you.
  • Solve problems step by step rather than feeling overwhelmed.
  • Stay connected: talk to family, friends, a church or community group, or a co-worker.
  • Look after your body: rest, food, exercise.
  • Learn from experience: ask what the setback taught you.
  • Keep hope: remind yourself of difficulties you overcame before.

Managing stress

Signs of too much stress include poor sleep, headaches, irritability, drinking more, and losing interest in things. Try simple methods: slow breathing, a short walk, writing your worries down and making a plan, and talking to someone. If stress or sadness continues for weeks, or you have thoughts of harming yourself, seek help from a clinic, a doctor, your employer's wellness programme or a helpline such as SADAG.

Example

Nomsa applied for a team leader post and was not chosen. At first she felt hurt. She asked her manager for feedback, learned she needed more experience with records, took a short course and offered to help with the house records. A year later she was appointed. That is resilience.

Key points

  • Self-esteem is the opinion you hold of your own worth; it can be built at any age.
  • Replace negative self-talk with fair, realistic thoughts.
  • Use SMART goals and manage your time, emotions, money and health.
  • Be assertive: clear and respectful, neither passive nor aggressive.
  • Resilience means adapting after setbacks; seek help if stress continues.
